source.root_cause: FORMAT_STRING: User-controlled input buffer passed directly as format string to printf(buf) at 0x401471 in main, without sanitization. When check(buf) returns 0 (any input except 'printf_is_dangerous'), printf interprets embedded format specifiers (%p, %x, %s, %n) against its vararg stack/register view.
source.description: Format specifiers %p/%x in user input cause printf to read and output values from registers (rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9) and stack that would not normally be disclosed. arg3 (rcx register) contains a libc code address; arg4 (r8) contains a binary code address (0x4014f0); arg5 (r9) contains an ld-linux address.

chain: BUG-001: printf(buf) with user-controlled format string at 0x401471
User embeds %p/%x format specifiers in input
printf reads vararg arguments from registers (arg1=rsi, arg2=rdx, arg3=rcx, arg4=r8, arg5=r9) and stack (arg6+)
arg3 (rcx) = libc code address leaked to stdout
arg4 (r8) = 0x4014f0 binary code address leaked (No PIE confirmed)
INFO_LEAK: libc/stack/code addresses disclosed, defeating libc ASLR

controlled_element.what: Format specifiers in input buffer (%3$p, %4$p, %5$p select specific vararg positions)
controlled_element.how: Attacker sends input containing %p format specifiers; read_input reads up to 31 bytes from stdin into buf at [rbp-0x20]; check(buf) returns 0 for non-matching input; main calls printf(buf) which interprets the specifiers

preconditions.description: Input must NOT match 'printf_is_dangerous' (19 bytes) to reach the vulnerable printf(buf) path. Any other input triggers the format string vulnerability.
preconditions.necessity: The check() function gates the branch: matching input → print_flag (safe), non-matching → printf(buf) (vulnerable). This is trivially satisfied by any input except the exact 19-byte pattern.

preconditions.description: Format specifier characters (%) must be present in the input to trigger the leak. The read_input function does not filter or sanitize any characters.
preconditions.necessity: Without format specifiers, printf outputs the input as literal text with no memory disclosure.

preconditions.description: Printf's vararg view must contain sensitive addresses at reachable positions. arg3 (rcx) contains a libc return address from __libc_start_main call chain.
preconditions.necessity: The leaked values must be meaningful addresses (libc/code/stack) for the leak to be useful. GDB confirmed arg3 is inside libc's r-xp segment.

alias_key_findings.alias: rcx holds the return address from __libc_start_main's call to main (libc code address inside r-xp segment)
alias_key_findings.implication: Leaking arg3 via %3$p discloses a libc code address, allowing libc base calculation: libc_base = leaked_arg3 - known_offset. ASLR for libc is defeated.

alias_key_findings.implication: Leaking arg4 confirms No PIE (code at fixed 0x400000 range) and provides a known reference point.

mitigations.name: ASLR
mitigations.primitive_impact: ASLR randomizes libc base address between runs. However, the INFO_LEAK primitive defeats libc ASLR by leaking a libc code address (arg3), from which the base can be calculated. Binary ASLR is irrelevant (No PIE).

mitigations.name: PIE
mitigations.primitive_impact: No PIE means binary code/addresses are at fixed locations (0x400000 range). arg4 leak of 0x4014f0 confirms this. No need to leak binary base.

mitigations.name: FORTIFY_SOURCE
mitigations.primitive_impact: Binary compiled without FORTIFY_SOURCE. printf is plain printf (not __printf_chk), so %p/%n specifiers are fully functional without fortify restrictions.

evidence.description: Disassembly: lea rax,[rbp-0x20]; mov rdi,rax; mov eax,0; call printf@plt — user input buffer passed directly as printf format string argument.

Runtime: input '%3$p.%4$p.%5$p' produces output '0x7f1c02a4fb91.0x4014f0.0x7f1c02b5b380' — arg3=libc address (0x7f...), arg4=0x4014f0 (binary code), arg5=ld-linux address. All leaked via %p format specifiers.

GDB at printf call site: rcx=0x7ffff7ebeb91 (arg3), confirmed inside libc r-xp segment (0x7ffff7dcb000-0x7ffff7f53000). libc base=0x7ffff7da3000. r8=0x4014f0 (arg4, binary code). r9=0x7ffff7fca380 (arg5, ld-linux).

This byte is loaded via movzx eax, BYTE PTR [rax] at 0x401412 and compared to 0x0a (newline) at 0x401415. The read value is only used for this internal comparison and is never output to the attacker, making this a restricted 1-byte OOB read with no information leakage.

primitives.notes: PRIM-002 is THEORETICAL, not VERIFIED: the write code path exists at 0x401429 but the triggering condition (buf[-1] == 0x0a) cannot be met because buf[-1] is the high byte of the fixed return address 0x401448 (No PIE), which is always 0x00. This was confirmed by dynamic gdb evidence showing the comparison result (ZF=0, not equal). The write value is always 0x00 (null byte) and the write target is always buf[-1] or buf[-2] — neither the value nor the target is attacker-controlled. Even if the condition were met, this would only be a RESTRICTED_WRITE (1-byte null write at a fixed offset), not ARB_WRITE.

non_primitives.reason: OOB read at buf[-2] when read() returns -1 (I/O error). This requires read(0, buf, 0x1f) to return -1, which only occurs on actual I/O errors (EBADF, EIO, etc.). Since fd 0 is always valid stdin, read() returning -1 is not practically achievable through normal input methods (EOF returns 0, not -1). Even if achievable, buf[-2] = 0x00 (same fixed return address byte), so the same analysis applies: value read but not leaked, write condition unmet. Merged into PRIM-001 analysis as a theoretical variant.

The OOB read at buf[-1] does NOT constitute an INFO_LEAK. The byte read (0x00) is loaded into al and only used for an internal comparison (cmp al, 0x0a at 0x401415). It is never printed, returned, or otherwise observable by the attacker. The program output (' is not the correct answer.') does not contain the OOB read value. Therefore no information is leaked through this primitive.

The OOB read is strictly limited to buf[-1] (fixed offset -1 from buffer start) when read() returns 0, or buf[-2] (fixed offset -2) when read() returns -1. The attacker cannot control the read offset or target address — it is always a fixed negative index relative to the buffer. This does not meet the ARB_READ standard (target address must be attacker-controlled).

Even if the OOB write condition were met, the write target is always buf[-1] or buf[-2] (fixed offset from buffer), and the write value is always 0x00 (null byte). Neither the target address nor the written value is attacker-controlled. This is at most a RESTRICTED_WRITE (1-byte null write at fixed offset), not ARB_WRITE.
